Radar Cross-Section (RCS) measures how detectable an object is by radar, expressed in square meters or dBsm.
Modern stealth aircraft often have RCS values less than 0.0002 m².
RCS is defined mathematically as the ratio of scattered to incident electric field intensities at infinite distance.
Monostatic RCS assumes radar transmitter and receiver are co-located; bistatic RCS involves separate locations and is usually larger.
Geometric Optics (GO) approximates RCS by treating radar waves as rays and is valid when object size is much larger than radar wavelength.
Physical Optics (PO) accounts for wave properties like diffraction and assumes a perfectly conducting target in the far field.
Method of Moments (MoM) is the most accurate RCS calculation method, handling arbitrary geometries by solving integral equations numerically.
RCS varies with radar frequency and angle of incidence, requiring multiple wavelength testing for comprehensive stealth evaluation.
Fifth-generation stealth aircraft feature design elements such as flush bodies, V-tails, and internal weapon bays to reduce RCS.
The B-2 stealth bomber's design eliminated horizontal stabilizers, influencing future sixth-generation stealth aircraft.
RCS reduction is critical due to the increasing range and sophistication of radar-guided air-to-air and surface-to-air missiles.
Anechoic chambers lined with radar-absorbent foam are used for precise RCS measurement in controlled environments.
Bistatic RCS can be approximated from monostatic RCS using angular relationships but is more complex to calculate.
The Method of Moments uses surface patch models and basis functions to approximate current densities on the target surface.
Future air combat will rely heavily on sensor fusion and low observability features to maintain tactical advantages.
Stealth design also considers other detection methods such as infrared and electronic emissions beyond radar.
Stealth warships like the Zumwalt-class employ radar stealth but face challenges balancing stealth with operational performance.
The radar cross-section can be reduced by shaping surfaces to reflect radar waves away from the radar receiver.
Radar cross-section reduction techniques include shaping, radar-absorbent materials, and internal carriage of weapons.
The radar cross-section of an object is not a fixed value but varies with radar frequency, aspect angle, and radar type.
